back: Removing or replacing a cached copy when the source of truth changes.
A read that returns a value older than the latest committed write in the source of truth.
Pro: no coordination and self-healing. Con: staleness up to the full TTL, and shorter TTLs multiply database load.
Explicit delete on write for freshness, plus a TTL as a safety net for anything missed.
Finding every dependent key: profile, fragments, lists and feeds that embed the changed data.
A process reads the database's change stream (binlog, logical replication) and deletes affected keys after every commit, so no write path can forget.
A key that includes a version, e.g. product:42:v18. A write bumps the version; old keys become unreachable and age out.
A counter included in every key of a group (catalog:v8:...). Incrementing it invalidates the whole group at once.
Writer deletes, reader misses and reads old value, writer commits, reader sets old value. Cache stays stale until TTL.
A reader reads the old row before the commit and sets it after the delete. Needs a very slow reader; rare but real.
A token returned on a miss and required on the later set. A delete in between invalidates it, so stale sets are rejected.
Delete after the database update, then delete again after a short delay to remove anything a slow reader wrote back.

front: Why is updating the cache on write risky?
back: Two concurrent writers can update the cache in the opposite order to the database, leaving a wrong value until the TTL.

front: Why is delete on write safe under concurrent writers?
back: Delete is idempotent and order-independent: two deletes in any order leave the key empty, and the next read loads the latest value.
One extra miss after each write; on very hot keys that can trigger a stampede of reloads.
